Three points: pick-up, hold and break

Before each target the shooter sets three points. The pick-up point is where the eyes first see the target clearly. It is a little way out from the trap, not right next to it, where the clay is still only a blur. The hold point is where the muzzles wait at the call, usually on or just under the target's line, between the pick-up point and the break point. The break point is where the shooter plans to break the target.

Plan in this order. First choose the break point and set your feet for it. Then turn your upper body back and point the barrels at the hold point. Last, put your eyes on the pick-up point. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the stock stays down until the target appears, so there the hold point is simply where the barrels point while the gun is still low.

Typical errors with the break point: too far away means a fast, uncontrolled swing or a target already dropping. Too close, and there is too little movement: the shooter “pokes” at the target, pointing the gun slowly like a rifle instead of swinging it. With the hold point: too near the trap, the target overtakes the muzzles and the gun has to chase it. Too far out, there is too little room to move with the target, and the shooter pokes or stops the gun.

Tip: The exact hold point depends on the target and on your lead method. With maintained lead (barrels kept in front of the target the whole time) it is usually further out along the line. With swing-through (barrels start behind the target and overtake it) it is closer to the trap. Choose the break point where you see the target clearly and steadily, before it drops behind trees. Your coach will help you set all three points.

You “read” a target, that is, work out its path, speed and distance, while it is shown before shooting (the presentation). In Sporting™ the referee shows each trajectory to the first shooter of the squad. On request, the shooter on the stand can see each target of the menu again, at most twice. In Compak® Sporting by squad, the singles and then the simultaneous doubles are shown only once a day, in the morning, for the first squad. After a break of more than 10 minutes, the singles are shown again. More on viewing: Viewing the targets.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

In Sporting™ it is up to you to break each target where the referee can see it. Watch for shooting limits: a target broken beyond such a boundary, or behind a natural obstacle, does not count. The referee decides this alone, and the decision cannot be appealed.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 9 · Break targets where the referee can see

Key points

  • Pick-up = eyes; hold = muzzles; break = where the target is broken.
  • Plan from the break point backwards: feet, hold, eyes.
  • The hold point is usually between pick-up and break, on or just under the line.
  • Hold too near the trap and the gun chases; too far out and it has no room to move.
  • Read targets while they are shown; in Sporting™ break them where the referee can see, inside the shooting limits.

Did you know?

If you look too close to the trap, the target looks like a streak because the eye has not yet locked on. That is why the pick-up point is a little away from the trap.

Stand Talk

  • Coach Where are you taking it?

    Meaning: The coach asks where the shooter plans to break the target.

  • Coach Move your hold point halfway back to the trap.

    Meaning: Hold the muzzles closer to the trap, at half of the current distance.

  • Coach Look further out — pick it up where it's sharp.

    Meaning: Move the eyes away from the trap to where the target is first seen clearly.

  • Coach Hold a little lower, just under the line.

    Meaning: Keep the muzzles slightly below the target's path at the call.

For the interpreter
  • “Where are you taking it?” asks for the break point; “kill point” is a neutral synonym.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which point is about the eyes, not the gun?

    1. Hold point
    2. Break point
    3. Pick-up point
    4. Insertion point
    Answer

    Pick-up point

    The pick-up point is where the eyes first see the target clearly; the hold point is for the muzzles.

  2. What usually happens if the hold point is too close to the trap?

    1. The referee calls No Bird
    2. The gun has to chase the target
    3. The gun has almost no room to move
    4. The target slows down
    Answer

    The gun has to chase the target

    Too near the trap, the target leaves at full speed past the muzzles, so the gun has to chase it. Too little room to move is the problem of a hold point too far out.

  3. In Sporting™, the shooter on the stand asks to see the presentation again. What is the maximum per target of the menu?

    1. Two targets
    2. None: no repeats are allowed
    3. As many as the shooter wants
    4. Exactly five
    Answer

    Two targets

    The referee will show it again if asked, but no more than twice per target on the menu.
